what_its_for: This medicine helps your body make more white blood cells after you receive chemotherapy (cancer treatment). Chemotherapy can lower your white blood cell count, which makes it easier for you to get serious infections. Pegfilgrastim-cbqv works by telling your bone marrow to produce more infection-fighting white blood cells to help keep you safe.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under your skin, usually in your stomach area, upper arm, or thigh. Your doctor or nurse will give you the injection, or they may teach you how to give it to yourself at home. If you are giving it yourself, always rotate the injection site so you do not use the same spot twice in a row. Do not inject into skin that is red, bruised, tender, or hard. The prefilled syringe is for one-time use only — never reuse or share it with anyone else. If you have questions about how to inject yourself, ask your healthcare team to show you before trying it at home.
dosing: The usual adult dose is one injection (6 mg) given once per chemotherapy cycle. Your doctor will tell you exactly when to take it — it is typically given at least 24 hours after your chemotherapy is finished. Do not take it within 14 days before your next chemotherapy treatment. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose timing may be different depending on your treatment plan.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled injection or forget to give yourself the shot, contact your doctor or nurse right away. Do not try to make up for a missed dose on your own without guidance. Your healthcare team will tell you the best time to give the injection to stay on track with your chemotherapy schedule.
storage: Keep this medicine in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it — if it accidentally freezes, you may thaw it once in the refrigerator, but throw it away if it freezes a second time. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. You may keep it at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for no more than 3 days if needed. Throw it away if it has been at room temperature for more than 3 days. Keep out of reach of children. Dispose of used syringes in a puncture-resistant sharps container — never throw loose needles in the trash.
what_to_avoid: Do not receive this injection within 14 days before or 24 hours after chemotherapy. Avoid areas of skin that look irritated, bruised, red, or have scars or stretch marks. Tell your doctor if you are taking lithium, as it may increase white blood cell counts and interact with this medicine. Avoid shaking the prefilled syringe, as this can damage the medication. Do not use the medicine if it looks cloudy, discolored, or contains visible particles.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: sudden or severe pain in your left upper stomach area or shoulder (this could be a sign of a serious spleen problem); difficulty breathing, fever, or signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or dizziness; severe bone or muscle pain that does not improve with over-the-counter pain medicine; unusual bruising or bleeding; painful, swollen joints or skin sores (possible signs of a rare blood vessel condition); signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or feeling very unwell; or any sudden new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working within 24 to 72 hours after your injection by stimulating your bone marrow. Your white blood cell count will typically rise within a few days and usually peaks about 3 to 4 days after the injection. Your doctor will do blood tests to check your white blood cell levels during your treatment to make sure the medicine is working properly.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The risks to an unborn baby or nursing infant are not fully known. Children: This medicine can be used in children for certain conditions, but the dose is based on body weight. Ask your child's doctor for specific instructions. Older adults: This medicine appears to work similarly in older adults, but always tell your doctor about all your health conditions and medicines. Sickle cell disease: Tell your doctor if you have sickle cell disease, as there have been rare reports of serious sickle cell crises in patients with this condition who used similar medicines. Kidney or liver problems: No dose adjustment is typically needed, but inform your doctor of any kidney or liver issues.
